statement: Exactly one of these five statements about a positive whole number n is false. (1) n is a multiple of 6. (2) n is a multiple of 9. (3) n is a multiple of 4. (4) n is less than 50. (5) n is odd. What is n?

choices.misconception: I trusted statement (5), so I kept the statements that fit an odd number, a multiple of 9 below 50, and picked 9, not noticing that two statements are then false.
I decided statement (2) was the false one and took the smallest multiple of both 6 and 4, forgetting that 12 is not odd either.
I decided statement (3) was the false one and took the smallest multiple of both 6 and 9, forgetting that 18 is not odd either.
I decided statement (4) was the false one and took the first multiple of 36 above 50, but 72 is even, so statement (5) is false too.

hints: Which statements cannot both be true?
An odd number cannot be a multiple of 6 or of 4. So if statement (5) were true, at least two statements would be false. Decide which statement is the false one first.
Statement (5) is the false one, so n is a multiple of 6, of 9 and of 4, and it is less than 50.

solutions.reliable: If n were odd, it could not be a multiple of 6 or of 4, so statements (1) and (3) would both be false, which is one too many. So statement (5) is the false one, and the other four are true. Then n is a multiple of 6, 9 and 4, which means a multiple of 36, and n is less than 50. The only such positive whole number is 36. Check: 36 is a multiple of 6, 9 and 4, it is less than 50, and it is not odd, so exactly one statement is false. The transferable idea: when exactly one statement is false, find two statements that clash; the false one must be among them.

whyOnTest: 'Exactly one is false' puzzles test reading the condition precisely and finding statements that cannot all hold together.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
